claim: Tuberculosis (TB) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remains a leading cause of death from an infectious disease worldwide.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remains a leading cause of death from an infectious disease worldwide (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2022

claim: Approximately 2 billion people worldwide are latently infected with Mtb and represent a reservoir of future active disease.
source: Despite the availability of the Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) TB vaccine, approximately 2 billion people worldwide are latently infected with Mtb and represent a reservoir of future active disease (Trunz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trunz et al., 2006

claim: BCG is the only licensed TB vaccine and has been in use since the 1920s.
source: BCG is the only licensed TB vaccine and has been in use since the 1920 s, with close to 100 million infants vaccinated annually worldwide (Trunz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trunz et al., 2006

claim: Close to 100 million infants are vaccinated annually worldwide with BCG.
source: BCG is the only licensed TB vaccine and has been in use since the 1920 s, with close to 100 million infants vaccinated annually worldwide (Trunz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trunz et al., 2006

claim: BCG protects against TB meningitis and miliary TB in children.
source: BCG protects against TB meningitis and miliary TB in children, but lacks efficacy against pulmonary TB in adults (Martinez et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez et al., 2022

claim: BCG lacks efficacy against pulmonary TB in adults.
source: BCG protects against TB meningitis and miliary TB in children, but lacks efficacy against pulmonary TB in adults (Martinez et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez et al., 2022

claim: Bacterial peptidoglycan (PG) is detected by the PRRs NOD-1 and NOD-2.
source: Bacterial peptidoglycan (PG) is one such PAMP, and it is detected by the PRRs NOD-1, which recognizes the D-isoglutamate diaminopimelate (iE-DAP) segment of PG, and NOD-2 which detects the related muramyl dipeptide (MDP) portion of PG (Li and Wu, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Wu, 2021

claim: NOD-1 recognizes the D-isoglutamate diaminopimelate (iE-DAP) segment of PG.
source: Bacterial peptidoglycan (PG) is one such PAMP, and it is detected by the PRRs NOD-1, which recognizes the D-isoglutamate diaminopimelate (iE-DAP) segment of PG, and NOD-2 which detects the related muramyl dipeptide (MDP) portion of PG (Li and Wu, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Wu, 2021

claim: NOD-2 detects the muramyl dipeptide (MDP) portion of PG.
source: Bacterial peptidoglycan (PG) is one such PAMP, and it is detected by the PRRs NOD-1, which recognizes the D-isoglutamate diaminopimelate (iE-DAP) segment of PG, and NOD-2 which detects the related muramyl dipeptide (MDP) portion of PG (Li and Wu, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Wu, 2021

claim: Activation of NOD-1 triggers the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines through nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways.
source: Activation of NOD-1 triggers the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines through nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways and similarly, NOD-2 activation leads to upregulation of NF-κB activity (Caruso et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caruso et al., 2014

claim: NOD-2 activation leads to upregulation of NF-κB activity.
source: Activation of NOD-1 triggers the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines through nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways and similarly, NOD-2 activation leads to upregulation of NF-κB activity (Caruso et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caruso et al., 2014

claim: Pathogenic mycobacteria including Mtb, M. bovis, and the M. bovis-derived BCG strains possess an immune subversion system which enzymatically masks NOD-1 antigenic structure through amidation.
source: While many gram-negative pathogens express abundant levels of the NOD-1 ligand iE-DAP (Caruso et al., 2014), pathogenic mycobacteria including Mtb, M. bovis, and the M. bovis-derived BCG strains possess an immune subversion system which enzymatically masks NOD-1 antigenic structure through amidation, thereby enabling escape from NOD-1 mediated immune containment (Maitra et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caruso et al., 2014 and Maitra et al., 2019

claim: The enzyme pair encoded by the murT-gatD operon forms a glutaminase and an amidotransferase complex, which amidates iE-DAP to form iQ-DAP, thus avoiding NOD-1 detection.
source: The enzyme pair encoded by the murT (Mb3739, in M. bovis)-gatD (Mb3740) operon forms a glutaminase and an amidotransferase complex, which amidates iE-DAP to form iQ-DAP, thus avoiding NOD-1 detection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Amidation of D-isoglutamate to D-isoglutamine during PG maturation in mycobacteria is required for subsequent PG cross-linking.
source: As amidation of D-isoglutamate to D-isoglutamine during PG maturation in mycobacteria is required for subsequent PG cross-linking, MurT and GatD are important for mycobacterial cell wall integrity and genetic screens have confirmed their essentiality for in vitro survival (de Wet et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2021; Shaku et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Wet et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2021; Shaku et al., 2023

claim: MurT and GatD are important for mycobacterial cell wall integrity.
source: As amidation of D-isoglutamate to D-isoglutamine during PG maturation in mycobacteria is required for subsequent PG cross-linking, MurT and GatD are important for mycobacterial cell wall integrity and genetic screens have confirmed their essentiality for in vitro survival (de Wet et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2021; Shaku et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Wet et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2021; Shaku et al., 2023

claim: Genetic screens have confirmed the essentiality of MurT and GatD for in vitro survival.
source: As amidation of D-isoglutamate to D-isoglutamine during PG maturation in mycobacteria is required for subsequent PG cross-linking, MurT and GatD are important for mycobacterial cell wall integrity and genetic screens have confirmed their essentiality for in vitro survival (de Wet et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2021; Shaku et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Wet et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2021; Shaku et al., 2023

claim: Following ATc induction, the relative mRNA levels of the full length murT transcript were 1000-fold lower in rBCG::iE-DAP when compared with the uninduced rBCG strain.
source: We showed that following ATc induction, the relative mRNA levels of the full length murT transcript were 1000-fold lower in rBCG::iE-DAP when compared with the uninduced rBCG strain (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Activation of the CRISPRi platform in rBCG::iE-DAP with ATc [100–500 ng/ml] resulted in reduced growth in a concentration dependent manner.
source: Activation of the CRISPRi platform in rBCG::iE-DAP with ATc [100–500 ng/ml] resulted in reduced growth in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c

claim: CRISPRi mediated inhibition of murT-gatD transcription in rBCG::iE-DAP by supplementation of growth media with an increasing concentration of ATc [0–500 ng/ml] resulted in growth inhibition of the recombinant strain.
source: CRISPRi mediated inhibition of murT-gatD transcription in rBCG::iE-DAP by supplementation of growth media with an increasing concentration of ATc [0–500 ng/ml] resulted in growth inhibition of the recombinant strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c

claim: Knockdown of a MurT homologue in Mycobacterium smegmatis (MSMEG_6276) revealed a growth defect upon CRISPRi mediated MSMEG_6276 depletion.
source: This is consistent with earlier knockdown of a MurT homologue in Mycobacterium smegmatis (MSMEG_6276) which revealed a growth defect upon CRISPRi mediated MSMEG_6276 depletion (Shaku et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shaku et al., 2023

claim: rBCG::iE-DAP cells displayed a wrinkled outer-cell wall structure, sometimes with indentations.
source: As shown in Figure 1c, SEM revealed a well-formed typical mycobacterial outer cell wall structure in WT BCG, whereas rBCG::iE-DAP cells displayed a wrinkled outer-cell wall structure, sometimes with indentations.
evidence: Supported by SEM data shown in Figure 1c

claim: Quantification of SEM fields revealed a 70% increase in the frequency of bacilli with cell wall defects in rBCG::iE-DAP relative to the WT BCG.
source: Quantification of SEM fields revealed a 70% increase in the frequency of bacilli with these defects in rBCG::iE-DAP relative to the WT BCG (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1d

claim: TEM revealed a typical multi-layered mycobacterial cell wall outline with visible layers in WT BCG in comparison to the defective cell wall structure in rBCG::iE-DAP, without a clear cell wall outline.
source: Consistent with this, TEM revealed a typical multi-layered mycobacterial cell wall outline (Mahapatra et al., 2008), with visible layers in WT BCG in comparison to the defective cell wall structure in rBCG::iE-DAP, without a clear cell wall outline as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation to Mahapatra et al., 2008

claim: A 65% increase in the frequency of wall defects in rBCG::iE-DAP compared with the WT BCG strain was observed upon counting individual cells in TEM fields.
source: Upon counting individual cells in TEM fields, we observed a 65% increase in the frequency of wall defects in rBCG::iE-DAP compared with the WT BCG strain (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1f

claim: MurT-GatD knockdown was associated with a 2- to 16-fold decrease in the minimal inhibitory concentrations of the recombinant strain for amoxicillin-clavulanate, meropenem, vancomycin, and ethionamide.
source: Indeed, as shown in Table 1, MurT-GatD knockdown was associated with a 2- to 16-fold decrease in the minimal inhibitory concentrations of the recombinant strain for amoxicillin-clavulanate, meropenem, vancomycin, and ethionamide, each of which targets either PG biosynthesis or PG-dependent accessory glycolipids.
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Table 1

claim: BODIPY-FL vancomycin displayed complete cell wall labeling of the rBCG::iE-DAP cells, in contrast, only the poles of WT BCG cells were labeled.
source: As shown in the confocal fluorescence micrographs in Figure 1g, BODIPY-FL vancomycin displayed complete cell wall labeling of the rBCG::iE-DAP cells, in contrast, only the poles of WT BCG cells were labeled.
evidence: Supported by confocal fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1g

claim: Polar elongation of BCG cells results in the relative abundance of new, uncross-linked PG at the cell poles.
source: This corresponds to the known polar elongation of BCG cells and the relative abundance of new, uncross-linked PG at the cell poles (Aldridge et al., 2012; Joyce et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aldridge et al., 2012; Joyce et al., 2012

claim: Labeling of the MurT-GatD depleted cells showed a greater incorporation of the tetrapeptide fluorophore than in WT BCG.
source: As seen in Figure 1h, labeling of the MurT-GatD depleted cells showed a greater incorporation of the tetrapeptide fluorophore than in WT BCG.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1h

claim: Labeling of PG extracted from WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP with an amine reactive fluorescent dye revealed decreased amidation of PG upon MurT-GatD depletion.
source: We further assessed this reduced amidation by labeling of PG extracted from WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP with an amine reactive fluorescent dye, which binds amine (NH2) groups. This revealed decreased amidation of PG upon MurT-GatD depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), thus confirming that rBCG::iE-DAP displayed greater exposure of the iE-DAP, NOD-1 antigenic structure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: rBCG::iE-DAP displayed greater exposure of the iE-DAP, NOD-1 antigenic structure.
source: We further assessed this reduced amidation by labeling of PG extracted from WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP with an amine reactive fluorescent dye, which binds amine (NH2) groups. This revealed decreased amidation of PG upon MurT-GatD depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), thus confirming that rBCG::iE-DAP displayed greater exposure of the iE-DAP, NOD-1 antigenic structure.
evidence: Inferred from decreased amidation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: nod-1 and nod-2 expression was present at basal levels in non-activated and uninfected cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, nod-1 and nod-2 expression was present at basal levels in non-activated and uninfected cells as previously shown (Juárez et al., 2012; Rommereim et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and citations to Juárez et al., 2012; Rommereim et al., 2020

claim: WT BCG infection did not induce significant changes in nod-1/2 expression.
source: WT BCG infection did not induce significant changes in nod-1/2 expression and E. coli infection led to increased expression of both NOD receptors in both IFNγ activated and non-activated macrophages, as expected.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: E. coli infection led to increased expression of both NOD receptors in both IFNγ activated and non-activated macrophages.
source: WT BCG infection did not induce significant changes in nod-1/2 expression and E. coli infection led to increased expression of both NOD receptors in both IFNγ activated and non-activated macrophages, as expected.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: Infection with rBCG::iE-DAP led to an ~15-fold increase in NOD-2 expression in IFNγ-activated macrophages.
source: Infection with rBCG::iE-DAP led to an ~15-fold increase in NOD-2 expression in IFNγ-activated macrophages, an ~55-fold and ~200-fold increase in nod-1 expression in both non-activated and IFNγ-activated THP-1 macrophages, respectively (Figure 1i, j).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1i

claim: Infection with rBCG::iE-DAP led to an ~55-fold increase in nod-1 expression in non-activated THP-1 macrophages.
source: Infection with rBCG::iE-DAP led to an ~15-fold increase in NOD-2 expression in IFNγ-activated macrophages, an ~55-fold and ~200-fold increase in nod-1 expression in both non-activated and IFNγ-activated THP-1 macrophages, respectively (Figure 1i, j).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1j

claim: Infection with rBCG::iE-DAP led to an ~200-fold increase in nod-1 expression in IFNγ-activated THP-1 macrophages.
source: Infection with rBCG::iE-DAP led to an ~15-fold increase in NOD-2 expression in IFNγ-activated macrophages, an ~55-fold and ~200-fold increase in nod-1 expression in both non-activated and IFNγ-activated THP-1 macrophages, respectively (Figure 1i, j).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1j

claim: Dose-dependent inhibition of growth of rBCG::iE-DAP was observed at day 5, with 500 ng/ml ATc resulting in an ~three fold difference in growth inhibition of rBCG::iE-DAP in comparison to WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP without ATc supplementation.
source: Dose-dependent inhibition of growth of rBCG::iE-DAP was observed at day 5, with 500 ng/ml ATc (the maximum concentration used) resulting in an ~three fold difference in growth inhibition of rBCG::iE-DAP in comparison to WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP without ATc supplementation (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Activation of rBCG::iE-DAP by supplementation of growth media with ATc resulted in a dose-dependent increase in TNFα expression in comparison to WT BCG in IFNγ-activated BMDMs.
source: Activation of rBCG::iE-DAP by supplementation of growth media with ATc resulted in a dose-dependent increase in TNFα expression in comparison to WT BCG in IFNγ-activated BMDMs. However, this was statistically insignificant between strains, while TNFα expression remained low for both WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP strains when used for infection of unactivated BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: TNFα expression remained low for both WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP strains when used for infection of unactivated BMDMs.
source: Activation of rBCG::iE-DAP by supplementation of growth media with ATc resulted in a dose-dependent increase in TNFα expression in comparison to WT BCG in IFNγ-activated BMDMs. However, this was statistically insignificant between strains, while TNFα expression remained low for both WT BCG and rBCG::iE-DAP strains when used for infection of unactivated BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: BCG trains macrophages in a NOD-2 dependent manner and as a result, killing of Mtb is enhanced if the trained cells are exposed to Mtb at a later stage.
source: WT BCG trains macrophages in a NOD-2 dependent manner and as a result, killing of Mtb is enhanced if the trained cells are exposed to Mtb at a later stage (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; Kaufmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; Kaufmann et al., 2018

claim: Heat-killed rBCG::iE-DAP trained macrophages displayed increased control of Mtb H37Rv compared to heat-killed WT BCG trained macrophages and MDP trained macrophage.
source: As shown in Figure 2b, heat-killed rBCG::iE-DAP trained macrophages displayed increased control of Mtb H37Rv compared to heat-killed WT BCG trained macrophages and MDP trained macrophage.
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Macrophages derived from LPS stimulated monocytes did not control Mtb growth.
source: Macrophages derived from LPS stimulated monocytes did not control Mtb growth.
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Activation of CRISPRi in rBCG::iE-DAP with Dox resulted in a dose-dependent reduction of rBCG::iE-DAP growth.
source: Activation of CRISPRi in rBCG::iE-DAP with Dox resulted in a dose-dependent reduction of rBCG::iE-DAP growth (Figure 2c, d), which was corroborated when growth was assessed by CFU counts while WT BCG was not affected by Dox supplementation (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 2c, d

claim: WT BCG was not affected by Dox supplementation.
source: Activation of CRISPRi in rBCG::iE-DAP with Dox resulted in a dose-dependent reduction of rBCG::iE-DAP growth (Figure 2c, d), which was corroborated when growth was assessed by CFU counts while WT BCG was not affected by Dox supplementation (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 2c, d

claim: Administration of 1 mg/kg/day Dox resulted in a significant reduction in growth of rBCG::iE-DAP in the lungs of the mice.
source: Administration of 1 mg/kg/day resulted in a significant reduction in growth of rBCG::iE-DAP in the lungs of the mice (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Recovered rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli formed similar CFU counts on media with or without Kan.
source: We also plated lung homogenates on media containing Kan and found that recovered rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli formed similar CFU counts on media with or without Kan and PCR amplification of the dCas9 allele from recovered rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli revealed retention of the CRISPRi plasmid and the bacilli were responsive to ATc treatment (Figure 2f, g).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2f, g

claim: PCR amplification of the dCas9 allele from recovered rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli revealed retention of the CRISPRi plasmid.
source: We also plated lung homogenates on media containing Kan and found that recovered rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli formed similar CFU counts on media with or without Kan and PCR amplification of the dCas9 allele from recovered rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli revealed retention of the CRISPRi plasmid and the bacilli were responsive to ATc treatment (Figure 2f, g).
evidence: Supported by PCR data shown in Figure 2f, g

claim: At 8 weeks post infection, rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli recovered from the lungs of infected mice formed small colonies on solid agar in comparison to recovered WT BCG bacilli, indicative of the long-term efficacy of 1 mg/kg/day Dox in vivo for CRISPRi activation.
source: Similarly, as shown in Figure 2h, i, at 8 weeks post infection, rBCG::iE-DAP bacilli recovered from the lungs of infected mice formed small colonies on solid agar in comparison to recovered WT BCG bacilli, indicative of the long-term efficacy of 1 mg/kg/day Dox in vivo for CRISPRi activation.
evidence: Supported by colony morphology data shown in Figure 2h, i

claim: rBCG::iE-DAP infected mice displayed slight increased survival compared to WT BCG-infected mice, but this data was not significantly different from WT BCG-infected mice.
source: Although rBCG::iE-DAP infected mice, either receiving Dox or not, displayed slight increased survival, this data was not significantly different from WT BCG-infected mice.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 3b

claim: rBCG::iE-DAP upon CRISPRi activation is not more attenuated than WT BCG and does not cause more disease in SCID mice compared to WT BCG.
source: This suggested that rBCG::iE-DAP upon CRISPRi activation is not more attenuated than WT BCG and does not cause more disease in SCID mice compared to WT BCG.
evidence: Inferred from survival data shown in Figure 3b

claim: The weights of the different groups remained within 80–100% of baseline with few non-significant differences at week 6.
source: We assessed the percentage weight change of mice receiving Dox relative to the no-Dox groups and found that the weights of the different groups remained within 80–100% of baseline with few non-significant differences at week 6 (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by weight data shown in Figure 4b

claim: At week 4 post-infection, the WT BCG+Dox group displayed significantly lower lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group.
source: As seen in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, at week 4 post-infection, the WT BCG+Dox group displayed significantly lower lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group, while the WT BCG without Dox-treatment and the rBCG::iE-DAP with or without Dox-treatment groups displayed similar lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group.
evidence: Supported by lung weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: The WT BCG without Dox-treatment and the rBCG::iE-DAP with or without Dox-treatment groups displayed similar lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group at week 4 post-infection.
source: As seen in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, at week 4 post-infection, the WT BCG+Dox group displayed significantly lower lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group, while the WT BCG without Dox-treatment and the rBCG::iE-DAP with or without Dox-treatment groups displayed similar lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group.
evidence: Supported by lung weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: The WT BCG+Dox group displayed significantly lower spleen weights compared to the Saline+Dox group at week 4 post-infection.
source: Similarly as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, the WT BCG+Dox group displayed significantly lower spleen weights compared to the Saline+Dox group while the WT BCG without Dox-treatment and the rBCG::iE-DAP with or without Dox-treatment groups displayed similar spleen weights compared to the Saline+Dox group.
evidence: Supported by spleen weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: Analysis of lung and spleen bacterial burdens at 4 weeks post infection revealed that rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox was superior to WT BCG and WT BCG+Dox in protecting against Mtb challenge in the lungs.
source: Analysis of lung and spleen bacterial burdens at 4 weeks post infection revealed that rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox was superior to WT BCG and WT BCG+Dox in protecting against Mtb challenge in the lungs and reduced bacterial burden in the spleen similar to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox.
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4c

claim: rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox reduced bacterial burden in the spleen similar to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox at 4 weeks post infection.
source: Analysis of lung and spleen bacterial burdens at 4 weeks post infection revealed that rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox was superior to WT BCG and WT BCG+Dox in protecting against Mtb challenge in the lungs and reduced bacterial burden in the spleen similar to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox.
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4d

claim: At 8 weeks post Mtb challenge, the rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox group displayed reduced lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group and the WT BCG vaccinated group.
source: Also as seen in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a at 8 weeks post Mtb challenge, the rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox group displayed reduced lung weights compared to the Saline+Dox group and the WT BCG vaccinated group indicative of control of bacterial burden
evidence: Supported by lung weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: Analysis of lung bacterial burden corroborated findings at 4 weeks that rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox was superior to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox in controlling Mtb growth in the lung at 8 weeks post Mtb challenge.
source: and indeed, analysis of lung bacterial burden corroborated findings at 4 weeks that rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox was superior to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox in controlling Mtb growth in the lung (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4c

claim: At week 8, WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox vaccination both displayed waning efficacy in this model.
source: At week 8, WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox vaccination both displayed waning efficacy in this model, as previously shown (Henao-Tamayo et al., 2015; Dwivedi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4c and citations to Henao-Tamayo et al., 2015; Dwivedi et al., 2022

claim: In the spleen, rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox displayed similar efficacy to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox for control of infection compared to the Saline+Dox group at week 8.
source: In the spleen, rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox displayed similar efficacy to WT BCG or WT BCG+Dox for control of infection compared to the Saline+Dox group (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4d

claim: rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice presented with early increased lung inflammation compared to WT BCG+Dox vaccinated mice.
source: As shown in Figure 5a, b, histopathological analysis of haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained lung samples from the vaccinated and Mtb challenged mice indicated that rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice presented with early increased lung inflammation compared to WT BCG+Dox vaccinated mice.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 5a, b

claim: At 8 weeks post infection, rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice presented with increased inflamed sections of lung area compared to WT BCG+Dox immunized mice suggestive of sustained inflammation for control of infection.
source: At 8 weeks post infection also, rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice presented with increased inflamed sections of lung area compared to WT BCG+Dox immunized mice suggestive of sustained inflammation for control of infection (Figure 5c, d).
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 5c, d

claim: The increased early inflammation in rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice is reflective of early induction of anti-tuberculous immune responses, which were able to control growth early before establishment of infection.
source: The increased early inflammation in rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice is reflective of early induction of anti-tuberculous immune responses, which were able to control growth early before establishment of infection and the sustained inflammation at 8 weeks post challenge is suggestive of enhanced immune responses during chronic disease stage which enable control of disease progression as shown in Figure 4d.
evidence: Inferred from histopathology and CFU data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 4d

claim: The sustained inflammation at 8 weeks post challenge is suggestive of enhanced immune responses during chronic disease stage which enable control of disease progression.
source: The increased early inflammation in rBCG::iE-DAP+Dox immunized mice is reflective of early induction of anti-tuberculous immune responses, which were able to control growth early before establishment of infection and the sustained inflammation at 8 weeks post challenge is suggestive of enhanced immune responses during chronic disease stage which enable control of disease progression as shown in Figure 4d.
evidence: Inferred from histopathology and CFU data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 4d

claim: BCG does not provide protection against TB infection in adults and has failed to eradicate the disease.
source: However, BCG does not provide protection against TB infection in adults and has failed to eradicate the disease (Dockrell and Butkeviciute, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dockrell and Butkeviciute, 2022

claim: BCG possesses several immune evasion mechanisms similar to those used by Mtb during infection to avoid immune killing that limit its efficacy as a vaccine.
source: Also, there is evidence that BCG possesses several immune evasion mechanisms similar to those used by Mtb during infection to avoid immune killing that limit its efficacy as a vaccine (Guinn and Rubin, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guinn and Rubin, 2017

claim: rBCG strains further attenuated by deletion of immune evasion genes such as sapM, nuoG, or zmp1 show enhanced immunogenicity and efficacy against Mtb infection in animal models.
source: For example, rBCG strains further attenuated by deletion of immune evasion genes such as sapM (Festjens et al., 2019), nuoG (Gengenbacher et al., 2016), or zmp1 (Sander et al., 2015) among others, have been developed and these show enhanced immunogenicity and efficacy against Mtb infection in animal models.
evidence: Supported by citations to Festjens et al., 2019; Gengenbacher et al., 2016; Sander et al., 2015

claim: Selective chemical removal of lipids from BCG (i.e. delipidation of BCG) has shown the ability to enhance BCG efficacy in mice.
source: Selective chemical removal of these lipids from BCG (i.e. delipidation of BCG) has shown the ability to enhance BCG efficacy in mice (Moliva et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moliva et al., 2019

claim: A CRISPRi based rBCG (rBCG::CRISPRi-AftC) designed for the truncation of the anti-inflammatory cell wall associated lipoglycan – lipoarabinomannan (LAM) into the pro-inflammatory lipomannan derivative (LM) upon CRISPRi mediated depletion of the enzyme arabinofuranosyltransferase C (AftC) was shown to enhance the immunogenicity of BCG by upregulating the expression of TNFα.
